title: The Window · 6
paragraphs: But what had happened?
Someone had blundered.

Starting out of her musing, she gave meaning to words she had been holding in her mind, meaningless, for a long stretch of time. “Someone had blundered”—the line from Tennyson’s “The Charge of the Light Brigade.” She fixed her shortsighted eyes on her husband, who was now bearing down on her, and gazed steadily until, as he came close, she could see (the jingle paired itself off in her head) that something had happened; someone had blundered. But she could not for the life of her think what.

He shivered; he quivered. It had all been shattered, destroyed: all his vanity, all his pleasure in his own splendor as he rode, deadly as a thunderbolt, fierce as a hawk, at the head of his men through the valley of death. Stormed at by shot and shell, boldly we rode and well, flashed through the valley of death, volleyed and thundered—only to charge headlong into Lily Briscoe and William Bankes. He quivered; he shivered.

Not for the world would she have spoken to him. She knew the signs: his eyes turned away, and a curious gathering-in of his whole person, as if he were wrapping himself up and needed privacy in which to get his balance back. They told her he was outraged and in anguish. She stroked James’s head; she passed on to him what she felt for her husband. As she watched him color the white dress shirt of a gentleman in the Army and Navy Stores catalogue yellow with his chalk, she thought what a delight it would be to her if he turned out to be a great artist; and why shouldn’t he? He had a splendid forehead. Then, looking up as her husband passed her once more, she was relieved to find that the ruin was veiled. Domestic life had won; habit was crooning its soothing rhythm. So when he stopped deliberately at the window as his turn came round again, and bent down, teasing and whimsical, to tickle James’s bare calf with a sprig of something, she scolded him lightly for having sent off “that poor young man,” Charles Tansley. Tansley had had to go in and write his dissertation, he said.
“James will have to write _his_ dissertation one of these days,” he added ironically, flicking his sprig.
Hating his father, James brushed away the tickling sprig with which Mr. Ramsay was teasing his youngest son’s bare leg, in that way of his that was a mix of sternness and humor.
Mrs. Ramsay said she was trying to finish these wretched stockings so she could send them to Sorley’s little boy tomorrow.
There wasn’t the slightest chance in the world that they could go to the Lighthouse tomorrow, Mr. Ramsay snapped out irritably.
How did he know? she asked. The wind often changed.

It enraged him, the extraordinary irrationality of what she had just said, the folly of the female mind. He had ridden through the valley of death, had been shattered, had shivered; and now here she was defying the facts, letting his children hope for something utterly impossible—telling lies, in effect. He stamped on the stone step. “Damn you,” he said. Yet what had she actually said? Only that tomorrow might be fine. And so it might.
Not with the barometer falling and the wind due west.

To her it was a horrible outrage against human decency: to pursue the truth with so astonishing a disregard for other people’s feelings, to rip apart the thin veils of civilization so wantonly, so brutally. She gave no answer. Dazed and blinded, she bowed her head, as though letting the pelting of jagged hail, the soaking of dirty water, splash all over her without one word of reproach. There was nothing to be said.
He stood by her in silence. At last, very humbly, he said that he would walk over and ask the Coastguards, if she liked.
There was nobody she revered as she revered him.

She was perfectly willing to take his word for it, she said. It only meant they wouldn’t need to cut sandwiches—nothing more. Being a woman, she naturally had people coming to her all day long with one thing or another; this one wanted this, that one wanted that; the children were growing up; she often felt she was nothing but a sponge, soaked through with human emotions. And then he said, Damn you. He said, It must rain. He said, It won’t rain; and at once a Heaven of safety opened in front of her. There was no one she revered more. She wasn’t good enough to tie his shoelaces, she felt.

Already ashamed of that outburst, of the way he had waved his hands while charging at the head of his troops, Mr. Ramsay gave his son’s bare legs one more rather sheepish prod. Then, as though she had given him permission, he plunged off into the evening air. The movement struck his wife as oddly like the great sea lion at the Zoo, who tumbles over backward once he has swallowed his fish and flounders away, so that the water in the tank slops from one side to the other. The air was already thinning; it was drawing the substance out of the leaves and hedges, but, as if to make up for it, it gave the roses and pinks a luster they had lacked all day.
“Someone had blundered,” he said again, striding off, up and down the terrace.

How extraordinarily his tone had changed, though! It was like the cuckoo—“in June he gets out of tune”—as though he were trying out, groping toward, some phrase to suit a new mood, and, with nothing but this one to hand, made do with it, cracked as it was. Yet it sounded absurd, “Someone had blundered,” spoken that way, almost like a question, with no conviction at all, in a singsong voice. Mrs. Ramsay couldn’t help smiling, and before long, sure enough, pacing up and down, he hummed it, let it go, and went quiet.

He was safe; his privacy had been given back to him. He paused to light his pipe and glanced once at his wife and son in the window. You know how, on an express train, you lift your eyes from a page and see a farm, a tree, a huddle of cottages, as if they were a picture illustrating the printed words, a confirmation of them, and you go back to your book strengthened and content. Just so, without his really making out either his son or his wife, the sight of them gave him strength and contentment, and blessed his effort to reach a perfectly clear grasp of the problem that now absorbed the energies of his splendid mind.

It was a splendid mind. Suppose thought is like a piano keyboard, divided into so many notes, or like the alphabet, set out in twenty-six letters in order. Then his splendid mind could run through those letters one after another, firmly and accurately, with no trouble at all, until it arrived at, let us say, the letter Q. He reached Q. Hardly anyone in the whole of England ever gets to Q. Pausing a moment here by the stone urn with the geraniums in it, he caught sight of his wife and son together in the window, but far, far off now, like children gathering shells, divinely innocent, busy with small trifles at their feet, and somehow wholly unprotected against a doom that he could see coming. They needed his protection; he gave it to them. But what about after Q? What comes next? Beyond Q lie a number of letters, and the last of them can barely be seen by mortal eyes; it glimmers red, far away. Z is reached only once in a generation, by one man. Still, getting to R would be something. Here, at least, was Q. At Q he dug in his heels. Of Q he was certain. Q he could prove. If Q, then, is Q—R—At this point he knocked the ash out of his pipe with two or three ringing taps against the ram’s horn that formed the urn’s handle, and carried on. “Then R …” He steeled himself. He clenched himself.

Then came to his aid the qualities that would have saved a ship’s crew adrift on a scorching sea with a flask of water and six biscuits—endurance and fairness, foresight, devotion, skill. Well then, R is—what is R?

Like the leathery eyelid of a lizard, a shutter flickered down over his intense gaze and hid the letter R. In that flash of dark he could hear people saying it—that he was a failure, that R was beyond him. He would never get to R. Once more, on to R. R——

Once again the qualities came to his aid that, on some desolate expedition across the frozen solitudes of the Polar regions, would have made him the leader, the guide, the counselor—the one whose temper, neither hopeful nor gloomy, looks calmly at what lies ahead and meets it. R——

Again the lizard’s eye flickered. The veins stood out on his forehead. The geranium in the urn leapt startlingly into view, and there among its leaves, whether he wanted to or not, he could see that old, obvious division of men into two kinds. On one side were the steady ones, plodding and persevering with superhuman strength, who go through the whole alphabet in order, all twenty-six letters, beginning to end. On the other were the gifted, the inspired, who by some miracle take in all the letters at once, in a single flash—the way of genius. Genius he did not have; he made no claim to it. But he had, or might have had, the power to go through every letter from A to Z, accurately and in order. In the meantime, he was stuck on Q. Onward, then—on to R.

Over him crept feelings worthy of a leader who, with the snow now beginning to fall and mist closing over the mountaintop, knows he must lie down and die before morning. They faded the color of his eyes, and even in the two minutes it took him to walk the length of the terrace, they gave him the bleached look of shriveled old age. But he would not die lying down. He would find some crag of rock, and there, with his eyes on the storm, straining to the last to see through the darkness, he would die on his feet. R he would never reach.

He stood stock-still by the urn, the geranium spilling over its rim. After all, he asked himself, out of a thousand million men, how many ever get to Z? Surely the leader of a forlorn hope, a doomed advance party, has the right to ask that, and to answer, without betraying the expedition following him, “One, perhaps.” One in a generation. Should he be blamed, then, for not being that one? so long as he has worked honestly, given everything in his power, until there is nothing left to give? And how long will his fame last? Even a dying hero may be forgiven for wondering, before he dies, how men will talk of him when he is gone. Perhaps his fame will last two thousand years. And what are two thousand years? (asked Mr. Ramsay ironically, staring at the hedge). What indeed, if you gaze down from a mountaintop across the long wastes of the ages? The very stone your boot kicks aside will outlast Shakespeare. His own small light would shine for a year or two, not very brightly, and would then be swallowed up in some larger light, and that in a larger one still. (He peered into the darkness, into the tangle of twigs.) So who could blame the leader of that forlorn party—which has, after all, climbed high enough to see the waste of the years and the stars perishing—if, before death stiffens his limbs so that he can no longer move, he lifts his numb fingers to his brow a little deliberately and squares his shoulders, so that the search party, when it comes, will find him dead at his post, a fine figure of a soldier? Mr. Ramsay squared his shoulders and stood very straight beside the urn.

If he stands like that for a moment, dwelling on fame, on search parties, on the cairns of stones that grateful followers will heap over his bones, who will blame him? And last of all, who will blame the leader of the doomed expedition if, after venturing to the very limit, spending his strength down to the final ounce, and falling asleep with little care whether he ever wakes, he now feels a pricking in his toes and realizes that he is alive—and that, on the whole, he doesn’t mind being alive, but wants sympathy, and whisky, and someone to hear the story of his sufferings right away? Who will blame him? Who will not be secretly glad when the hero lays his armor aside, and pauses by the window, and gazes at his wife and son? They are very far away at first, then little by little they draw nearer and nearer, until lips and book and head are plain before him, though still lovely and strange to him after the intensity of his isolation, and the waste of the ages, and the perishing of the stars. And when at last he slips his pipe into his pocket and bows his magnificent head before her—who will blame him for paying homage to the beauty of the world?
